newsitem.title: UK: GUS posts 1st profit fall in 48 years.
newsitem.headline: GUS posts 1st profit fall in 48 years.

text.p: Retailer Great Universal Stores Plc, best known for its Burberry classic clothing, saw its shares dive on Thursday after reporting its first fall in half year profits in 48 years, partly attributed to its flagging mail order business.
Ans the group, Britain's premier mail order business, said it saw no significant signs of a second half upturn.
Higher costs, the strong pound and the decline in the role of agents in driving mail order sales were behind the slip in earnings of the group for the first time since 1949.

Pretax profits fell to 235.6 million pounds ($382 million) from 237.5 million in the six months to September 30, 1996. Sales rose to 1.21 billion pounds from 1.20 billion. The dividend was increased to 5.5 pence, from 5.0 pence.
GUS, the British market leader in mail order, had already flagged the profit fall in October, but the downbeat trading statement hit its shares, which fell 22.5 pence to 653.5.
Chairman Lord Wolfson of Sunningdale said trade was still difficult in the home shopping division, which saw both sales and profits fall in the first half.

He told a news conference higher costs and a fall in the number of agents who bring in orders from catalogues such as Kays, and Great Universal, were behind the profit decline. He said there had been no significant change in the second half.
Traders said the damage done by a strong pound to earnings from GUS's overseas retailing interests, including Burberry, also hit the stock.
"The statement didn't make very pretty reading," said one.
Last month GUS broke with its deeply conservative past by buying U.S. information services firm Experian for $1.7 billion, its first acquisition in more than two decades.
The change of pace followed the arrival of Lord Wolfson of Sunningdale as chairman in August, taking over from his older cousin Lord Wolfson of Marylebone.
There has been speculation of more changes to come, especially as the new chief is also chairman of highly successful fashion retailer Next Plc, which also has a mail order business.

Wolfson acknowledged that Britain's mail order was ripe for consolidation and that smaller branded direct mail catalogues -- already big in the United States -- were likely to take over from the agency-style big books offering a vast array of goods.

He said GUS was interested in buying Freemans, just put up for sale by rival Sears Plc, the third biggest player in the business. But he feared a bid by market leader GUS would trigger a monopoly investigation.
Privately-owned Littlewoods has been tipped as a likely buyer, along with German home shopping group Otto Versand and France's La Redoute.
Wolfson said GUS was looking at expanding direct mail either by acquisition, a franchising deal or by starting its own direct mail brand from scratch.

"We are looking at what the route is to enter the small niche catalogue business," Wolfson told journalists. Chairman of Burberrys Eric Barnes said the group was already exploring launching a Burberry catalogue.
But when asked if GUS would buy Next, Wolfson said that would be too expensive. ($1=.6161 Pound)
